articles.title: All-Star Superman Writer Grant Morrison Delivers His Verdict on Supergirl and Jason Momoa's Lobo
articles.summary: Comic book legend Grant Morrison has delivered his verdict on the DC Universe’s Supergirl movie — and in doing so had some choice words for Jason Momoa’s Lobo.
articles.body:
Comic book legend Grant Morrison has delivered his verdict on the DC Universe’s Supergirl movie — and in doing so had some choice words for Jason Momoa’s Lobo.

Morrison, whose comic book series All-Star Superman influenced James Gunn’s Superman movie, talked about Supergirl via his Substack, Xanaduum . In the post Morrison said Supergirl “wasn’t terrible but wasn’t especially great either,” and praised Millie Alcock for doing a “credible job” with Kara Zor-El.

So far, so good. But things go downhill from there. Morrison singled out Jason Momoa’s portrayal of Lobo — a role Momoa has said he was the perfect fit for — as “one of the worst performances I’ve ever seen in a film and quite baffling.” Ouch.

DC Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

The anti-hero bounty hunter only appears in Supergirl in a supporting role, despite his prominence in the movie's marketing in the run up to release. Some have said Lobo feels tacked on to Supergirl due to the fact he only has one scene with Kara. From IGN's Supergirl review :

The one scene he has with Kara has real reshoot energy. It’s added on to a scene that didn’t need any extra motivation to get to the next scene, nor is he a particularly unique foil for Kara that propels her character in any meaningful way. He just happens to be looking for the same group of guys that Kara and Ruthye are after. The only real added value he gives the movie is a few (admittedly fun) one-liners. And maybe that’s all Lobo needs to be. Ultimately, he shows up to put his immortal stamp of approval on Kara’s actions, but that feels both unnecessary and more than a little pandering, and it leaves me not entirely sure what to do with him.

Morrison went on to say Supergirl falls apart in the second act, criticising the plot for not making sense. Here are his comments on Supergirl in full:

I watched Supergirl, which wasn’t terrible but wasn’t especially great either. All the best and most moving scenes involved Millie Alcock, and I thought she did a credible job. Jason Momoa, who I was actually looking forward to, was very disappointing as Lobo. It was, in fact, one of the worst performances I’ve ever seen in a film and quite baffling, as I know Momoa’s not usually that bad and Lobo seems like a character made for him to play. Go figure. Then the whole plot fell apart in Act 2 — all Supergirl had to do was bring Krypto with her to that yellow sun world, and the sun’s rays would have made the dog invulnerable again, easily able to shake off any toxin. They needn’t have bothered chasing after the dull and low level Romanian gangster baddie, Krem of the Yellow Hills, to get the antidote after all!

As most know, Supergirl suffered a disastrous box office run, making just $126 million from theaters globally. After last year’s Superman, that was a big disappointment for DC Studios, and left some questioning the future of the DCU itself. Gunn’s Superman follow-up, Man of Tomorrow, comes out next year with Alcock reprising her role as Supergirl. But before then the DCU continues with the last two episodes of well-received HBO show Lanterns, and body horror movie Clayface.

In August, Warner Bros. boss David Zaslav said Gunn was "focused on Man of Tomorrow" following the failure of Supergirl , working up to 18-hour days on the forthcoming sequel. Asked about the future of the DCU following Supergirl, Zaslav told investors that the DCU remained on-track, insisting the current slate "feels very good."

DC Studios co-CEO Peter Safran had previously commented on Supergirl's box office in an interview with The New York Times : "While Supergirl didn’t meet our box office expectations, it’s just one component of a broader, long-term strategy at DC Studios that we remain confident in,” he said.

As for the future of Momoa's Lobo, the Aquaman actor has said any Lobo solo movie must be rated R. "It's all I want and I promise, I do not have any interest in making a PG-13 Lobo movie," Momoa told Collider in June. "Will he be part of some other movies? If they want me, I'll be there. But if I make a solo movie, I'm not doing it unless it's rated R."

articles.title: Una estrella de la NBA advierte sobre el 'desplome' de la liga por el GTA 6: "Prepárense para noviembre"
articles.standfirst: Steven Adams anticipa un bajón por el lanzamiento del videojuego
articles.summary: Steven Adams anticipa un bajón por el lanzamiento del videojuego
articles.body: Que el lanzamiento del GTA 6 va a paralizar el mundo no es un secreto para nadie. Y es que próximo título de Rockstar Games será el lanzamiento de la década, ya que millones de personas en todo el mundo están esperando ansiosas poder volver a meterse en el universo de Grand Theft Auto. Tanto es así que en Estados Unidos se esperan pérdidas de millones de dólares por parte de las empresas por absentismo laboral el próximo 19 de noviembre coincidiendo con la salida del GTA 6. Pero esta bajada de rendimiento causada por el videojuego no va a afectar solamente a los talleres, las empresas informáticas, hospitales...también va a tener repercusiones en el mundo del deporte, donde los protagonistas, por su forma de vida, son habituales consumidores de videojuegos. Pero esto no lo decimos nosotros, lo dice Steven Adams, el pívot de Houston Rockets. Y es que el neozelandés, una de las estrellas de la liga durante los últimos años, siempre acostumbra a bromear, a afrontar las entrevistas y las ruedas de prensa con mucho sentido del humor, por eso estas declaraciones en las que avisa sobre un bajón en el rendimiento de la liga para noviembre. El culpable de todo esto, como decíamos antes, sería el GTA 6, el que llegará a nuestras vidas el 19 de noviembre: “Yo diría que deberían prepararse para noviembre. El rendimiento de la liga, en toda la liga, va a salir afectado porque sale GTA, así que mirad la NFL, mirad todas las ligas y observad cómo se desploman solo durante el mes de noviembre". Así, Steven Adams anticipaba un bajón que, por suerte, durará poco tiempo: "El rendimiento va a bajar, aunque debería volver a subir. La mayoría de los chicos, con suerte, terminarán el juego. El entrenamiento y los ojeadores también van a ser horribles solo durante noviembre, pero debería recuperarse en diciembre. Con suerte, debería estar bien.”

articles.title: McDonald's Tests Ads — or 'Post-Purchase Content' — for Other Brands on Menu Screens After You Place Your Order
articles.summary: McDonald’s is testing ads from other brands that appear on the digital menu screen after you place your order.
articles.body:
McDonald’s is testing ads from other brands that appear on the digital menu screen after you place your order.

Bloomberg reported that the fast food chain wants to make more money from its 13,700 restaurants across the U.S. by taking advantage of the period of time — whether that’s seconds or minutes — that customers spend waiting for their burgers.

A McDonald’s spokesperson told Bloomberg: “This limited menu board advertising pilot at select company-owned restaurants is exploring ways to share post-purchase content that customers may find helpful, relevant, or interesting, while ensuring the McDonald’s experience remains at the centre of every visit.”

Given 26 million Americans buy food from McDonald’s each day, and the chain reaches nearly 90% of the country’s population every year, you can see why it sees an opportunity here, even if its idea might rub some McDonald’s customers up the wrong way.

There’s extra context here: according to Bloomberg, McDonald’s sales aren’t growing quite as fast as they used to, and it faces rising costs. It plans to spruce up its restaurants, too, improving the quality of food and customer service.

Reaction to the ad news has been mixed. “They'll do anything except improve quality for the money,” one person on the foodnews subreddit commented. “Improve quality, portion and value? That's crazy talk! Let's annoy our customers by subjecting them to more advertising.”

“So McDonald’s is losing customers at a rapid rate and they're panicking trying to find methods in which to slow their descent down the s**t chute,” another person said. “They've already raised prices, reduced sizes, reduced quality, cut drink refills, raised point costs on the app, cut most of the good deals from the app, arguably have a value menu in name only, have made the lobby mostly inhospitable, AND removed the convenience of a front lobby employee.

“Instead of rectifying any of that, the new plan is to assault the senses of their remaining customers with ads for trash bags and lip balm. This is like something straight out of Cyberpunk.”

“Oh... thanks, McDonald's,” one person said, “like modern Americans, etc. aren't bombarded enough with ads as it is... you're really doing us a solid by forcing ads on a captive audience waiting in the drive-thru.”

There is no indication yet that this ad test will be rolled out to all stores nationwide.

Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images.

articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company Estimated to Have Sold 1 Million, With Nearly 70% on Steam
articles.summary: Star Wars Zero Company is estimated to have sold 1 million copies, with the majority of those sales coming from Steam.
articles.body:
Star Wars Zero Company is estimated to have sold 1 million copies, with the majority of those sales coming from Steam.

Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott took to social media to discuss the performance of Bit Reactor’s Star Wars strategy game, which was developed by former developers of XCOM at Firaxis.

69.9% of those 1 million sales came from Steam, with 19.9% on PlayStation, and 10.2% on Xbox / Xbox PC. Clearly, Steam is where it’s at for Zero Company, which Elliott estimates has generated around $50 million since last month’s launch.

The Best Droids in Star Wars Games, Ranked

This performance, Elliott said, is “respectable for this genre and during such a crowded period (even with the Star Wars brand attached).”

But does it meet publisher EA’s expectations? The company has yet to issue official sales figures for Zero Company or comment on its commercial performance. Now EA has gone private, it is under no obligation to share revenue figures with the market, so it’s unlikely we’ll find out.

What we do know is that Bit Reactor furloughed "many of its workers" before Zero Company even came out as it reportedly had "run out of most of its money just ahead of the launch of its first game." Bit Reactor told Game File it was a "difficult decision" made "before it was clear how the launch would go," insisting it was not influenced by EA or Star Wars rights holder Disney. Game File reported that 80% of Bit Reactor’s staff were furloughed, leaving a skeleton crew to address any post-launch bugs for Zero Company.

“It's SO GOOD, but it's niche,” Elliott added. “One thing limiting Zero Company’s sales, as with many Star Wars games, is that it’s only really popular in the West. Of Zero Company’s players, 90% are in North America or Europe, with under 5% in Asia.

“On Steam, the Chinese user reviews sit at 57% positive (versus an 82% global average), with many pointing to the lack of VO and localisation options. Star Wars has never had the pull in Asia that it has in the West, of course. But skipping proper localisation compounds that.”

What happens next? The latest Zero Company patch was released on September 10, but we haven’t heard from the studio since.

IGN's Star Wars Zero Company review returned a 9/10. We said: "Star Wars Zero Company is an excellent tactical game that does a fantastic job of slathering on the same cinematic look and feel we saw in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi games, incorporating strong characters and a storyline that's refreshingly centered on non-Force users and a non-traditional villain."

articles.title: Frodo's Back! Set Photos From The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum Offer Behind-the-Scenes Look at Prequel Movie
articles.summary: Warner Bros. has released set photos from The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum to celebrate Hobbit Day, revealing a first look at Frodo and the Shire.
articles.body:
Warner Bros. has released set photos from The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum to celebrate Hobbit Day, revealing a first look at Frodo and the Shire.

The prequel movie, currently filming in New Zealand with a release date of December 17, 2027, sees Elijah Wood reprise his iconic role as Frodo Baggins. This peek at the character, released on Warner Bros.' TikTok page , doesn’t tell us much other than Frodo looks a lot like Frodo should. Unfortunately, as we’re only seeing Frodo’s back, we can’t see Wood’s face in character. I suspect that’s because the de-aging technology will be applied later on, so showing the character in full now wouldn’t accurately represent what fans will see in theaters.

But we do see plenty of Hobbits in the shire, as well as director and Gollum actor Andy Serkis working a camera. It’s all very nostalgic and pretty.

The Hunt for Gollum will reunite Serkis with his fellow Lord of the Rings co-stars Ian McKellen as Gandalf and the aforementioned Wood as Frodo, with Lee Pace reprising his role as elven king Thranduil from The Hobbit film trilogy. New additions to the cast include Fifty Shades of Grey actor Jamie Dornan, who takes over from Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie actress Anya Taylor-Joy, who plays a new "lethal elf" named Seren .

Serkis hit the headlines in July when he discussed The Hunt for Gollum's use of AI to digitally de-age some of The Lord of the Rings' aging stars , who need to look younger than they did 25 years ago in Fellowship of the Ring. "There’s a little bit of de-aging for some of the characters and machine learning is part of the process," Serkis said.

The movie revolves around various characters tracking down Gollum in order to discover the location of the One Ring. This time period is briefly shown during Fellowship's prologue, and covered briefly in Tolkien's original writings.

The Lord of the Rings Movies in (Chronological) Order

"I'm leaving him to it," The Lord of the Rings director Peter Jackson said previously of Serkis taking the helm. "I'm there to help if I can help, if I can be of assistance at certain times, I'm there. But I'm giving him as much freedom as I can, because giving Andy freedom to make that movie will result in the best possible film."

articles.title: Avengers: Endgame Encore Leaks Reveal New Ending and Additional Scenes That Connect to Avengers: Doomsday, Including Several Unannounced Cast Members
articles.summary: Four new scenes included in Avengers: Endgame Encore have leaked online, including a tweaked ending to the 2019 Marvel blockbuster.
articles.body:
Four new scenes included in Avengers: Endgame Encore have leaked online, including a tweaked ending to the 2019 Marvel blockbuster.

These additional extras have been designed to link Endgame directly to the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, and also to encourage theatregoers to rewatch the last Avengers film all over again to swell Marvel's coffers - er, I mean, to prep themselves for what's next.

Warning! Spoilers for Avengers: Endgame Encore follow:

Inevitably, footage has emerged from early screenings of Avengers: Endgame Encore showing the new scenes in full, which Marvel is now scrambling to scrub from social media. However, IGN has reviewed numerous copies of the scenes today before they were deleted from X/Twitter via copyright claim — thereby confirming their legitimacy.

Most notably, the scenes include multiple characters whose appearance in Doomsday had not previously been revealed. Since these extra moments are believed to have been filmed during Doomsday's production, it's now likely we'll be seeing more of these characters in December, when Doomsday itself arrives.

Avengers: Doomsday Trailer: First Look at Doctor Doom

The first extra scene acts as a new ending to Endgame, and merges directly with the pre-existing finale that fans already know and love: Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter reunited, sharing a dance, and settling down to a quiet life together.

Except the couple's quiet moment together is now interrupted by a knock at their door. Cautiously, Peggy opens it to reveal Loki, who greets the couple, as Steve looks surprised.

A few things here are immediately obvious — this is the version of Loki who has joined the TVA (the Time Variance Authority, essentially Marvel's multiverse police) but before he ends up becoming the all-powerful replacement of Kang. All of this fits with long-held leaked information that suggests Loki moves Steve and Peggy (and their son) to another branch of the multiverse for their own protection, several years before the main events of Doomsday take place.

During Endgame Encore's credits, the first all-new scene features Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner (and briefly, off-screen, the Hulk). This appears to be our first confirmation that the character will indeed appear in Avengers: Doomsday, after last being seen in bad shape at the end of Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

Indeed, this scene picks up a little while after Hulk is taken away, seemingly out of action following a destructive stint as his green alter ego. Now secluded in an old military bunker two miles underground, Banner records a video where he begins to discuss his work creating a new stabilizing serum. And, of course, he states that no one can get into the bunker to disturb.

Unfortunately, his video (and his work on that serum) are interrupted by the arrival of Doctor Doom into the bunker to disturb him. While kept offscreen, we hear Robert Downey Jr's voice say that he's come to "collect" Banner, as the scientist seemingly morphs into the Hulk once more. Has Doom enslaved Hulk, or sought to absorb his power somehow? We'll have to wait and see.

The Most Surprising Avengers and Marvel Characters Not Announced for Doomsday

The TVA Realizes The Multiverse is Collapsing

The next all-new scene is set within the TVA, presumably in the time after Loki has ascended to godhood. His former colleagues Mobius (Owen Wilson), Casey (Eugene Cordero) and Ouroboros (Ke Huy Quan) all panic as they spot a pair of Earths from different universes about to collide, and which begin to attack each other. One of these Earths is Universe-1005, the Fox X-Men universe, which ties into long-held leaks that the mutant team has been surviving incursions by wiping out other universes first. (I sure hope they don't have to destroy a universe with any other beloved Marvel character in!)

Things quickly get worse, however, as the TVA team quickly realizes that the entire multiverse is collapsing, with thousands of universes now at risk of being annihilated through incursions.

While some involvement of the TVA in Doomsday seemed likely, none of these characters have previously been confirmed to return for the film. Indeed, none have been seen since the finale of Loki, which wrapped up in 2023. Tara Strong's animated Miss Minutes also features here, too.

At the end of Endgame Encore's credits, one final snippet sees Doctor Doom hammering his metal mask into shape. This is a clear and obvious nod to Iron Man (also played by Robert Downey Jr.!) who created his first mask in the same way, and a reference to the original ending of Endgame, which featured the same hammer sounds heard here (which come from the first 2008 Iron Man film).

Maybe the Russos always knew this post-credits tease would eventually be changed to feature Doctor Doom! Or, maybe, this is just a really clever callback.

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on December 18, and I'm genuinely more excited to see it after watching all of these. Are you headed to Avengers: Endgame Encore to catch them on the big screen?

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: The Best Video Game Movies and TV Shows
articles.summary: From Netflix animations to live-action survival horrors, these are the best video game movies and TV shows.
articles.body:
Is the era of the bad video game adaptation finally over? There have been enough great movies and TV shows over the past few years to suggest that the curse has been lifted. Gone are the days of mediocre Tomb Raider films being as good as we had it and live-action Mario movies haunting our collective nightmares. For clarity, this is separate from our older Best Video Game Movies list, which you can check out here if you so wish. From Netflix animations to live-action survival horrors, here are what we think are the 10 best video game movies and TV shows.

Veteran British actor Bill Nighy voicing the equally legendary Mewtwo is just one of the reasons why Pokemon Detective Pikachu is an enjoyable time. Tim (Justice Smith) and Lucy’s (Kathryn Newton) adventure to find the former’s missing father unravels a mystery worthy of this world’s greatest detective. Voiced with charm by Ryan Reynolds, Detective Pikachu is just the pocket monster for the job, as he leads us through Ryme City and a view into the world of Pokemon as we’ve never seen before.

Few games have as flashy action as Capcom’s Devil May Cry does, so it’s no surprise that the Netflix series based on the games has some of the sharpest animation seen on the platform. Demon hunter Dante is tasked with keeping the Earth safe from the Hellish threats lurking in a neighboring realm, and stylishly unloads thousands of bullets doing so. Season 1 builds up to a truly bonkers finale of the sort the source material demands, as Hoon Lee’s villainous White Rabbit steals the show, while 2026’s second season shines the spotlight on the enigmatic Vergil. It’s never subtle, but certainly entertaining, even if it’s not the best Netflix adaptation on our list.

If at the turn of the century you’d have told us that Jim Carrey and Keanu Reeves were starring in a movie together, we would have been very excited. If you’d then told us that they’d be playing Dr Robotnik and Shadow the Hedgehog, we’d have been confused, but likely still excited. The fact that the Sonic films are seemingly the only ones that can coax Carrey out of retirement will always be confusing, but we’re not complaining too much when the third of this trilogy has given us some of his best work in a long time. Sonic the Hedgehog 3 is the best of a series that only seems to be getting better over time, as they up the stakes, absurdity, and quality of Ben Schwartz’s loveable blue blur’s adventures with each outing.

A prestige TV adaptation of The Last of Us always felt inevitable. The original game is very much structured like a show, after all. And when it comes to the first season of HBO’s series, that destiny looked to be one fulfilled to great success, with Pedro Pascal and Bella Ramsey slotting into the shoes of beloved characters Joel and Ellie. If it had stopped there, you’d likely see this show near the very top of this list. But following an uneven retelling of the, admittedly, much more complex source material that is The Last of Us Part 2, the jury remains out on whether it will be able to do the full story justice by the time the series finishes. Still, there’s no denying the quality of the production on show, with that first season’s journey across a post-apocalyptic America providing some of the best moments, and episodes, of television of the past few years.

Quantity over quality would’ve been the way most described Resident Evil’s big-screen efforts of the past. Then Zach Cregger arrived. The Weapons and Barbarian director took the essence of what has made Capcom’s survival horror series so enduring and translated it into 90 minutes of non-stop action. Each and every moment of its riveting runtime is aimed at provoking an instinctive reaction from us, whether that be to laugh or scream, sometimes managing to do both within seconds of each other. Bryan’s evening from hell through Raccoon City encapsulates what it’s like to play through one of the games in a way that none of the previous attempts ever did. It’s scary. It’s funny. It’s absurd. It’s Resident Evil.

Cyberpunk: Edgerunners takes Night City’s streets from the 2020 RPG and tells a moving tale that’s as resonant as its striking animation. Yes, it’s all based on Mike Pondsmith’s tabletop game, widely considered a keystone of the genre, but this is a TV show based as much on CD Projekt’s creation as anything, with whole city blocks and characters redrawn in this prequel. In some ways, it delivers the title’s themes in a manner that’s even stronger than in the game, thanks to how well-realised its lead, David, and the characters that surround him are. It’s wonderfully additive to CD Projekt’s world — an extension of a place so many of us have gotten lost in, but seen through different eyes.

Netflix’s Castlevania series was consistently fantastic over its four-season run, elevating the storytelling ability of the games and giving a new dimensionality to characters that had previously been built with gameplay first in mind. It deliciously plays in the grey areas between good and evil, with varying factions and motivations all in play up until its satisfying conclusion. Borrowing from the Game of Thrones playbook of never letting any character feel safe from their fate, it’s a thrilling interpretation of the Konami series, and a trailblazer when it comes to what’s possible with video game adaptations.

Sparked by Arcane Season 1’s eye-catching inventiveness and heartfelt character work, a whole new legion of fans found themselves enmeshed in the League of Legends universe, if in a completely unexpected way. Riot’s MOBA undoubtedly has a huge, devoted player base, but it's the developer work outside of the arenas that is so impressive, whether that be the toe-tapping catchiness of virtual bands such as K/DA, or Arcane, genuinely one of Netflix’s best shows, video game-related or not. Season 2 may not have quite lived up to the astronomical heights set by its first batch of episodes, but the artistry of animation studio Fortiche, combined with a coming-of-age story laced with rebellion and betrayal, still stands as one of the greatest translations of a video game into a different medium.

The writers and producers behind this Prime Video series hit the nail on the head when it came to adapting Bethesda’s RPG series. Fallout, the game series, is all about the world it's set in, from the quirky characters found within it to the oddities of its post-nuclear war locations. And so taking the vibe and feeling of wandering around the wasteland was always going to be the right move for the show, rather than simply retelling any of the game’s storylines. So far, we’ve had two seasons full of fan-favourite details that miraculously never quite feel like pandering, but instead use famous iconography and factions to tell their own tale. The best compliment you can give the show is that it feels just like watching a game you haven’t played yet, plucked from another corner of the Fallout universe. It’s reverent of its source material without feeling beholden to it, and as violent and funny as it needs to be for good measure.

Pokemon is so ingrained in our culture that it’s kind of difficult to recall where it all started. For many of us, it would have been with the animated series starring Ash Ketchum as an ambitious young trainer. Some of us would even have watched the first seasons of the show before we played any of the Game Boy games or swapped trading cards at school – so much so that you can almost be forgiven for not thinking of the original run of the anime as a video game adaptation (a beast that has gone on to realise over 1,300 episodes in its own right).

The series feels so in step with the games that they have influenced each other over time, especially in the mid- and late-’90s. Ash’s adventures with Squirtle, Charmander, Venusaur, and the gang wouldn’t exist without the release of Pokemon Blue, Red, and Green, but Yellow wouldn’t have followed soon after if Pikachu hadn’t become the show’s breakout star. It’s an ouroboros effect that created foundational memories for many growing up at the time, serving as a gateway into video games and Japanese animation for a whole generation. It’s almost so obvious that you forget it was an adaptation in the first place, but there’s no denying the massive impact Pokemon had, and the joy and tears shared when watching it.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: Jurassic World Evolution 3: Prehistoric East - Official Gobisaurus Gameplay Trailer - IGN
articles.summary: Meet the Gobisaurus in the latest Jurassic World Evolution 3: Prehistoric East trailer for the upcoming expansion for the dinosaur park management sim game. The Gobisaurus will be available as part of the Jurassic World Evolution 3: Prehistoric East DLC, available on September 29, 2026. articles.title: Nobody does it like Remedy
articles.summary: With Control Resonant, Alan Wake studio Remedy Entertainment moves its sci-fi franchise in a new, open-world direction.
articles.body: Video games have given us plenty of ways to traverse huge open worlds, but none have felt quite as oddly exhilarating as manipulating gravity in Control Resonant’s twisted version of New York City. It’s a game that lets you flip, twist, and fly through the air, while exploring settings that look ripped out of Inception. It’s as if you mashed up the meta storytelling of House of Leaves with the inventive platforming of Super Mario Galaxy and somehow turned it into a coherent experience. That strange combination is just the latest example of developer Remedy making games like nobody else out there. Resonant is a sequel to 2019’s Control — though the two games are designed to be played in any order — and is centered on a supernatural government agency known as the Federal Bureau of Control, or FBC. The original game followed new FBC director Jesse Faden as she tried to fight off a paranormal force known as the Hiss, which was invading the Oldest House, the FBC’s labyrinth headquarters. The sequel puts you in the role of her brother Dylan as the Hiss and other interdimensional threats start taking over Manhattan. A few things have changed in the sequel aside from the setting and protagonist. The big one is that Resonant is set in a relatively large open world, as opposed to the confines of the Oldest House. It’s a place that has been warped by the invading forces; buildings twist and bend in impossible ways, and sometimes gravity doesn’t behave as it should. The other major change is that while the original Control was mostly a shooter, Resonant is melee-focused, as Dylan wields a shapeshifting weapon that can mimic things like a whip or a hammer. [Media: Initially, Resonant plays much like a traditional open-world action game. Dylan has two main goals: to eradicate the forces invading New York, and to find Jesse, who has been missing since the events of the first Control game. He does this by taking on missions, defeating bosses, and exploring. For the first few hours I was disappointed because it all felt so familiar, which is the exact opposite of what I expect out of a Remedy game. From Control to Alan Wake, the studio is known for a distinct vibe that blends the tone of weird fiction with gameplay that heightens every emotion. Soon enough, though, Resonant opened up and became something truly wild. The Control games have something of a Metroid-style structure, limiting your progress until you have the right ability. And as soon as you gather those abilities, Resonant reveals what it truly is. You can temporarily fly, dash through the air, double jump, walk on walls and ceilings, and eventually warp to far-off ledges. When you combine and master these abilities — some take a bit of time to wrap your head around — you can zip around New York like some kind of strange superhero. Just moving around is thrilling, but these abilities are also put to use for some incredible platforming and puzzle sequences that test your ability to think spatially. Resonant also builds on the storytelling and worldbuilding that Remedy is known for. The Control franchise’s sci-fi setting is reminiscent of a handful of other properties, everything from Severance and the SCP Foundation, to the Southern Reach series and newcomers like Backrooms, with more than a dash of Twin Peaks. But it’s adapted in a way perfectly suited to video games. For Resonant, there’s the standard blockbuster campaign, which plays out through cutscenes and a lot of radio chatter between Dylan and his FBC handler Zoe. Like the rest of the game, the story starts out slow and simple before becoming something much stranger and more complex. It’s fleshed out by an absurd amount of supplementary material — field recordings, copious documents, instructional videos — that really bring the universe of Control to life. In most games, I skip these narrative add-ons; in Control, they’re a highlight of the experience because they’re so well done. The same goes for side quests. Even seemingly mundane tasks, like replacing light bulbs, can reveal strange and fascinating things. Seriously, this game gets weird; at various points, I was hailing a ghost taxi in a quest that played like The Exit 8, and talking to one of the aforementioned light bulbs in order to calm it down. All of that complexity is necessary to understand, even on a basic level, a story that involves alternate dimensions, impossible physics, multiple timelines, and some supernatural mold. [Image: Like its predecessor, Resonant is a very stylish game. Moving around and fighting nightmare creatures doesn’t just feel good, it looks and sounds amazing, with visual and audio effects that give the game a harsh, industrial vibe. There are platforming sequences that feel like interactive art exhibitions, and an entire section of the map that looks like if M.C. Escher became obsessed with the golden hour in NYC. The game even has an opening title sequence that looks ripped out of a hit HBO or Apple TV drama. This is all to say that Resonant excels at the things Remedy is best at — storytelling, worldbuilding, distinct visuals and sound design — while adding a new element in the form of the much more open navigation. There are a few parts of the game that get in the way of what’s great. It took me a while to warm up to Dylan as the protagonist because he is just so dull. I understand why, since he spent years of his life locked up by the FBC. But when you spend dozens of hours with a character, you want them to have some personality, even from the start. All I really know about Dylan is that he has superpowers, likes to draw, and is really close with his sister. While I mostly enjoyed the combat, it can be overwhelming, particularly toward the end when you’re bombarded with large numbers of enemies that take forever to kill. It’s tedious and drags down the experience, which led to me utilizing the game’s robust “assist” mode to tone down the difficulty. And although I love the movement and environments in Resonant, there’s a good chance you’ll find yourself lost at least a few times. When a world folds in on itself, a mini-map isn’t all that helpful. But if you enjoy the games Remedy makes, Resonant’s issues are a small price to pay. At a time when blockbuster games can feel increasingly similar, the Finnish developer is part of a small group of studios, like FromSoftware and Kojima Productions, that have retained a distinct vision while still releasing bold, ambitious games. The new game is especially notable after the high-profile failure that was FBC: Firebreak, a co-op Control spinoff that launched last year. Resonant twists the world of Control into something completely different — and in the process shows exactly what Remedy is capable of. Control Resonant launches on September 24th on the PS5, Xbox, and PC.

articles.title: Sony PlayStation Patent Would Solve System Problems With AI Vibe-Coded Patches
articles.summary: Anyone who's had a console knows that on a long enough timeline they will have some kind of technical bug that you need to troubleshoot, and Sony is trying to get around that reality with an AI tech support agent.
articles.body:
Anyone who's had a console knows that, on a long-enough timeline, they will have some kind of technical bug that you need to troubleshoot. Sony is trying to get around that reality with an AI tech support agent.

Sony has filed a patent for an AI that would keep an eye on your system, looking for any kind of red flags, and then use an LLM to write up a patch for your system to either preemptively fix the issue or to send a report to engineers at Sony. The problem is, that unless you can turn this feature off, all the data processed on your PlayStation would potentially be visible to this agent. It would likely need total access to successfully monitor a system for any and all hardware and software issues.

It's also possible that the system could make small issues into much larger ones. As Patentlyze found , the patent says "an automated system sending repair instructions to a device in your living room needs careful guardrails so a small hiccup does not become a larger one." After all, the PlayStation 5 (and likely the PlayStation 6) are just specialized computers, and there have been plenty of times that I've broken something by fixing a small problem that I probably could have just ignored (or wasn't a real problem to begin with).

The 100 Best PlayStation Games of All Time

There's also a possibility that, unless the LLM has particularly strong training and guardrails, that it could make a mistake when coding these on-demand patches, and accidentally brick people's PlayStations.

It's not clear when or if this patent will actually materialize into an AI tech support agent for your PlayStation. However, with the death of discs for the PlayStation 6 , it's likely that Sony's next generation console is going to require an always-on Internet connection to begin with. And with that constant communication with Sony's servers, an AI system like this would be trivial to implement. So if anything, I'd guess that this feature will make its debut with Sony's next-generation platform, which will hopefully give the company enough time to work out the logistics and privacy risks that are inherent to remote AI monitoring.

articles.title: Xbox Mythic Achievement Will Be Microsoft's Version of a Platinum Trophy — And It Has an Extravagant Unlock Sound
articles.summary: Microsoft is expected to imminently launch Xbox Mythic Achievements, its own version of PlayStation's platinum Trophies, and you can now hear how they will sound when unlocked.
articles.body:
Microsoft is expected to imminently launch Xbox Mythic Achievements, its own version of PlayStation's platinum Trophies, and you can now hear how they will sound when unlocked.

Xbox has previously confirmed plans to introduce its own method of tracking your full completion of a game — that is, when you have unlocked all of a title's 1,000 Gamerscore by nabbing every single Achievement.

Now, an update to the Xbox PC app has revealed the sound effect for an Xbox Mythic Achievement being unlocked, which has been discovered buried within the update's files. You can hear its rather majestic audio cue just below, courtesy of Xbox leaker Klobrille.

A new update for the Xbox PC App reveals: Xbox Mythic Achievement; plus symbol and unlock sound. The Xbox Mythic Achievement is expected to be a 100% Gamerscore game completion reward. pic.twitter.com/STLisa4ubz — Klobrille (@klobrille) September 22, 2026

A new update for the Xbox PC App reveals: Xbox Mythic Achievement; plus symbol and unlock sound. The Xbox Mythic Achievement is expected to be a 100% Gamerscore game completion reward. pic.twitter.com/STLisa4ubz

The sound is a suitably more grandiose version of the regular achievement unlock ping, which already can be heard in a more dramatic form when a rare achievement (owned by only a small percentage of players) is unlocked instead.

Microsoft's new Xbox Mythic Achievement effect is longer and more majestic still, lasting around 15 seconds as the audio wooshes in, builds, and then reverberates around. It's satisfying stuff, though whether it'll actually encourage you to grind for hours to get that full 1000G is entirely your choice.

Back in the day, Xbox Achievements were the first standardized reward system on a console platform, launching in 2005 back on the Xbox 360. The concept was so popular that Valve introduced Steam achievements in 2007, while Sony added Trophies to the PS3 in 2008.

While games typically share awards lists across platforms (so Xbox Achievements and PlayStation Trophy requirements are typically similar), Sony platforms have long featured the extra Platinum Trophy for most games, unlocked alongside your final regular Trophy. It is a signifier that you have truly mastered everything a game might have to offer, and fans' Platinum Trophy counts have themselves become something to collect and show off.

Microsoft is yet to say when Xbox Mythic Achievements will land across the Xbox ecosystem, but today's leak certainly suggests it won't be long now.

articles.title: Marvel Rivals Needs an Intervention
articles.summary: Poor balancing, toxic players, and a flawed approach to cosmetics have put Marvel Rivals in a bad place. It desperately needs an intervention to turn its troubles around.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Carlos Morales, who is a massive fan of Marvel whether it’s comics, movies, or video games. He’s sunk well over 1,000 hours into Marvel Rivals.

Marvel Rivals Season 10 is now available, and it’s coming at a time of crisis for NetEase’s premiere hero shooter. What was once a smash hit success on launch back in December of 2024 has now become a confused mess of developer priorities as more and more players drop off in favor of games with a clearer sense of direction. Making a live-service game work long term is a feat only a handful of dev teams have managed to achieve, and during its first year it seemed like Rivals was set to join that club. But between consistent balancing problems and a lack of integrity in competitive mode, NetEase’s penchant for predatory monetization creeping into the store, and controversies around character cosmetics that some players believe to be racially motivated, Rivals has found itself floundering when it should be hitting new heights.

These problems can’t be something that Marvel and Disney are too happy about, especially since Avengers: Doomsday , which is almost certain to be a financial success, is only a few short months away and could generate a large influx of new players. Let’s take a look at what’s gone wrong with Marvel Rivals, and what NetEase needs to do to turn things around.

To say that Rivals has had a recurring problem with balancing is something of an understatement. Although the game receives balance changes with each half-season, including a new patch that updated more than half the cast to start off Season 10, Rivals has often struggled to create a battlefield that feels entirely fair. Not that there’s anything wrong with a casual “anything goes” mentality to game design, but NetEase clearly wants Rivals to be a competitive game – it’s heavily pushing into the e-sports and tournament space, to the point of clogging up the main menu with tabs dedicated to those elements. Yet if NetEase really wants Rivals to be that kind of game, it needs to take a hard look at not just the current state of its characters, but its entire content release strategy.

Starting with Season 3, Rivals implemented an accelerated release schedule, with seasons shortened to two months and one hero released every month (Gorr being the only new hero in Season 10 is set to be an exception). This has resulted in many new heroes being released seemingly without being adequately playtested, with additions like Daredevil, Gambit, Elsa Bloodstone and Black Cat being utterly broken on release and needing multiple seasons worth of nerfs to get them even close to a reasonable state. The new team-up system introduced in Season 9 may have given most characters new tools, but it’s also snowballed the power creep to an outrageous degree, creating a battlefield littered with nonstop ability cooldowns and visual clutter instead of a meaningful neutral game.

Compounding these problems are NetEase’s flawed matchmaking algorithm, which often results in stomps instead of engaging matches, and the developer’s refusal to add significant penalties for toxic behavior in competitive mode. While cheaters do receive account bans, throwers and leavers are only slapped on the wrist with 15 minute suspensions, which hardly deters bad actors. NetEase recently announced it will implement “stricter penalties” for repeat offenders, but didn’t offer any details beyond increasing the duration of suspensions. I know this is a free-to-play game that depends on players routinely purchasing battle passes and costume bundles to stay afloat, so NetEase likely doesn’t want to shut out paying customers, but the lack of integrity in ranked play is detrimental to the intended strategy for the game’s future.

These problems have been so pronounced that many players on social media have even called for Zhiyong, the game’s lead combat designer, to be fired. While that may be several steps too far, such sentiments don’t materialize in a vacuum, and they’re only exacerbated by the game’s other issues, many of which stem from the cosmetics.

As mentioned previously, I’m well aware that free-to-play games like Rivals need to make money in their costume shop. And to be fair to NetEase, the game has been quite generous with free costumes and in-game units through seasonal events. However, the game has also been mired in controversy both for the more aggressive monetization strategies (a problem endemic to other NetEase games) and the uneven distribution of costumes among the character roster.

Gacha gambling events have become common for big skin releases, where players have a small chance of winning a full bundle by spending units to pop balloons containing individual items. This is a well-worn example of predatory monetization, luring players who might otherwise not have purchased a cosmetic with the potential to win something major for a fraction of the cost. That it’s a mechanic in a game where a large portion of the audience is presumably children is frankly reprehensible.

Regarding distribution, while certain popular characters getting more costumes than others does make financial sense, the disparity has become more pronounced in recent seasons. It’s been frustrating for players who feel that the devs are disrespecting comic book icons with decades of history. To use a recent example, the game’s incredibly popular Summer Swimsuit line of costumes caused an online firestorm when a swimsuit outfit for Storm was revealed to be of Epic rarity, when virtually every other swimsuit skin was a higher-grade Legendary. That Storm has received so few costumes despite being in the game since launch caused a contingent of fans to accuse NetEase of racial discrimination. The backlash was so fierce that Danny Koo, an executive producer at Marvel Games who oversees Rivals, was even called “Danny Koo Klux Klan” by fans on social media.

The controversy is a result of how little attention the game has given to its Black heroes, especially in comparison to white and Asian dev favorites like Psylocke, Invisible Woman, and Luna Snow. In response to the Storm situation, NetEase had to issue a statement saying her swimsuit costume would be upgraded to Legendary status and that Storm would receive more Legendary skins in the future. But that things even got that bad in the first place shows how aggrieved the game’s Black fanbase has become. That’s not even getting into the game’s almost non-existent Latino representation. While some may point to Namor, he’s more Indigenous Mesoamerican than Latino, and so the first proper Latin character in the game was not a superhero like Robbie Reyes’ Ghost Rider, Miles Morales, or one of the incarnations of White Tiger, but instead the villainous Hood, who is white in the comics and is portrayed as a sex pest in the game. Not great!

I want to make something clear: I love Marvel Rivals . I’ve been playing since the closed beta and it’s been my multiplayer game of choice ever since launch. It’s great fun as a casual game with friends, and I’ve climbed competitive mode to Celestial rank in several different seasons. I think the core gameplay is fantastic, and that the game mostly does justice to the cast and mythology of the Marvel universe. All that said, its many problems have eroded its positive aspects, and I believe NetEase needs to make an attitude adjustment if it wants to get the game back on track. What does that look like? I have some suggestions.

First, the balancing strategy needs to be reworked. The point of making balance changes is to eventually get to a place where you don’t need them anymore, so instead of making sweeping changes to “shake things up,” identify overpowered heroes and actually do something that permanently keeps them in line. The content schedule needs to be slowed down so that new heroes and modes can be adequately balanced and playtested before they’re released to the public. It would also be prudent for the next few seasons’ worth of new heroes to be exclusively in the tank and support classes, since the game is overflowing with DPS heroes. And while the new team-up system introduced in Season 9 was a needed shot in the arm, the numerous powerful cooldowns associated with team-ups definitely still need some tweaks to encourage more neutral gameplay.

Stricter penalties for toxic behavior in ranked need to be implemented. I would strongly suggest seasonal bans for repeat throwers and leavers so that ruining match integrity risks actual consequences. As for cosmetics, the gacha events should be retired. Buying a costume for my favorite hero (it’s Scarlet Witch, if you must know) should be something exciting instead of something frustrating. Focus on adapting fan favorite looks from the comics for underperforming heroes in the store. And while I know that certain heroes keep the lights on, consider giving one of the other characters a chance before greenlighting five more Legendaries for Luna Snow. Spreading the love around more when it comes to costume bundles will almost certainly pay off in the long run because you never know what untapped markets are just waiting to jump in.

I won’t pretend that fixing the game’s problems is as easy as I’m making it sound, but these steps would do a lot to help restore its reputation. NetEase is clearly capable of listening to its fanbase since it has done so many times in the past, and Avengers: Doomsday is right around the corner, so now is the time to make the changes the game needs to stay relevant in the market. Marvel Rivals may have lost its way, but that doesn’t mean it’s a lost cause.

Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .

articles.title: Sony Patent Would Let You Tap Your Card or Phone on Your PlayStation Controller to Make a Payment
articles.summary: Sony filed a patent called "video game controller-driven information transfer," and describes a controller with NFC capabilities, which would let you tap your phone or your credit card to your controller to send information to your console.
articles.body:
Both Sony and Microsoft have had a series of patents come out in the last week or so, and one of them would potentially bring NFC payments to the PlayStation 6.

Sony filed a patent called "video game controller-driven information transfer," which describes a controller with NFC capabilities that would let you tap your phone or your credit card to your controller to send information to your console. The most obvious use for this would be for payment, but it would also let you more easily import your PlayStation account to a new console.

Just like with any patent, there's no guarantee that this would result in an actual feature for any device, but if it did, it wouldn't be the first time this type of feature has existed. Pretty much every phone under the sun right now has similar functionality, which lets you tap your card to add it to your wallet, or tap bluetooth headphones to pair them without digging through the settings menu. So, it seems like a no-brainer to bring that functionality in some way to a console.

GTA 6 Special Edition PlayStation 5 DualSense Wireless Controller

There are of course some security issues that Sony would have to work out before implementing this, particularly if Sony wants you to import your whole account via this method. Without the right precautions, it'd be easy to grab someone's phone, tap it to your controller and effectively use their account.

Apple gets around this when setting up a new iPhone or iPad by bringing up a cloud that you have to scan with the new device's camera that will then give permission to import the account data. It's unlikely that Sony is going to put a camera in a controller, but a more simple option would be to have your phone display a pin number that you'd have to enter into the console to get past a security check.

What's particularly wild about this patent, though, is some of the rationale behind developing it. In the patent documentation, Sony talks about the traditional methods to input this data, like an on-screen keyboard or a QR code that you scan with your phone. But, then goes on to say "facilitating and coordinating these operations by performing multiple operational steps using multiple devices often causes performance of the video game console to suffer and/or one or more operations of the video game console to fail."

The idea here seems to be that importing all the account data through NFC will be more reliable than the current methods, and could prevent any kind of system failures during setup. NFC communication has become a lot better in recent years, to be sure, but whether it's going to make the system less prone to failure than typing in your data via a keyboard is something that'd I'd need to see to believe.

With all of the patents that have been coming out in the last couple weeks, it sure does seem like the next-generation consoles are actually on the way. Microsoft and Sony have both filed some pretty dystopian patents, but this one seems like it'd be genuinely useful. Either way, though, expect both the PlayStation 6 and Xbox Project Helix to be quite expensive, especially if they're announced amid the ongoing RAM crisis continues.

Starting off with the base PS5 you’ve got the choice of your standard performance and quality modes. Performance has the game running at a native lower fidelity that’s upscaled to 1440p but runs at a pretty solid target 60fps. Quality mode, on the other hand looks great, but comes at a cost a target frame rate of 30, and an upscaled output to 4k.The PlayStation 5 pro unlocks the game a bit more and offers three graphics modes that all output at an upscaled 4K resolution thanks to PSSR. Quality looks the best with hardware enables ray tracing, a sharp image, and a much more noticeable visual fidelity across the board. BUT you can’t have everything because it’s locked at a target 30fps. Performance offers a lower fidelity and no ray tracing but It runs at 60fps.Balanced is a mode I hope we see more often as it has improved visuals like quality mode, but squeezes out a few more frames per second. The only caveat is that you need a 120hz monitor to activate it. Regardless of what you choose, Control Resonant looks as good as it plays. Narrated by Nick Maillet.

The PlayStation 5 pro unlocks the game a bit more and offers three graphics modes that all output at an upscaled 4K resolution thanks to PSSR.

Quality looks the best with hardware enables ray tracing, a sharp image, and a much more noticeable visual fidelity across the board. BUT you can’t have everything because it’s locked at a target 30fps.

Performance offers a lower fidelity and no ray tracing but It runs at 60fps.

Balanced is a mode I hope we see more often as it has improved visuals like quality mode, but squeezes out a few more frames per second. The only caveat is that you need a 120hz monitor to activate it.

Regardless of what you choose, Control Resonant looks as good as it plays. Narrated by Nick Maillet.

articles.title: Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Might Be the Endgame I’ve Been Waiting For | IGN Preview
articles.summary: The first taste of Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance already has me salivating. The new tricks, new (and returning) monsters, and brand new suite of boosts are going to significantly disrupt how I do my builds, and how I approach hunts. Just thinking about it now has my synapses firing, and there are still so many weapons who're boosted actions I have yet to try, and who knows what new armor set bonuses might be ahead of us. The endgame of Monster Hunter Wilds was too easy, but this might be what Monster Hunter sickos are looking for.
articles.body:
Boost Drivers are a major new feature of this expansion.

The new monsters present challenging battles, just as I’d wanted.

Ascendance could be the endgame I’ve been wishing for after Wilds’s endgame was a bit too easy.

I liked Monster Hunter Wilds quite a bit at launch. The big open areas, the great visuals on the newest generation of consoles, and the cast of characters all made for an engaging adventure in the Forbidden Lands. But, like Tom so perfectly captured in his review , I felt let down by the challenge. The engaging loop of fighting tougher monsters to get better gear to fight tougher monsters, and so on, was missing that aspirational push that comes from difficult hunters demanding practice and gearing up, and it left me feeling a bit unsatisfied.

At Tokyo Game Show 2026 I went hands-on with Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance, the upcoming expansion, and holy smokes, what a difference two years makes. I took on a pair of monsters in some absolutely brutal fights, the sort that already have the build-crafting gears in my head turning. With the addition of new monsters, new areas, Master Rank hunts, and a dramatic expansion to the moveset of every weapon, this seems every bit the Monster Hunter World: Iceborne-style expansion I’d been hoping for.

My demo starts with no razzle-dazzle. I’m in the Grand Hub, with two missions to select. I start with the easier of the two, a hulking, winged Alpha Arakata. This fight takes place in the new Eyrie part of The Forbidden Lands, an area with strange flora reminiscent of Coral Highlands from Monster Hunter World. Floating layers of rock and interconnecting root systems forming bridges spiraling upwards add substantial vertically to the zone. As my trusty Seikret guides me to the monster, I take advantage of a series of updrafts to quickly climb to the upper layer, and I flock to Arakata, the noticeably larger and more dangerous looking alpha at the center.

For this hunt I’ve selected the Dual Blades, my personal weapon of choice most of the time. I leap from the back of my mount, and catch the target monster with a slash that sends me spinning along the length of its spine like a beyblade. I get off to a fast start, hacking at it after a nearby paratoad gets struck, and temporarily paralyzes the monster in retaliation. Once it regains control, the Arakata flaps its wings to get briefly aloft, then dives straight toward me like a missile, but I have a new trick up my sleeve...

One of the major new additions coming in Ascendance is Boost Drivers. On your hunts you now have a Boost Gauge that charges over time and while you attack, accumulate up to three charges of Boost. If you have at least one charge, you can activate Boost, which enhances the actions and attacks of your weapons. The effect is different for every weapon, in the case of my Dual Blades it give me new, ultra-rapid attacks, turns every dodge into damage-dealing acrobatics and, to the chagrin of this dive bombing Arakata, gives Dual Blades their first offset, attacks that counter and stagger incoming attacks, fully neutralizing damage and opening up yet more space for dealing damage.

The Alpa Arakata is no pushover, however. This is an all-new monster in the series, which means I’m learning on the fly. On the ground, it’s aggressive about slamming its wings and head, each covered in thick bone, forward towards me. But it’s at its most dangerous when it takes flight. It circles out of range of my short blades, then with little warning launches headfirst towards me at remarkable speed. It can quickly flap its wings to get height then charge ahead at any moment, which means no distance is “safe,” making it hard to predict. When it engages, it starts chaining dives to gather, and finishes by calling its flock, who join it flying in formation for a massive aerial dive-bombing.

It’s a back and forth fight, and eventually the Arakata flees. I chase on my Seikret, and I’m surprised to see that my overgrown bird-like mount has some new tricks too, which help navigate the aerial spaces of the Eyrie. It can now flap its wings, extending the time you spend aloft and gaining additional elevation. Seikret could always glide, but now they can tuck their wings tight, and rapidly accelerate through the air. Using this I keep close to my quarry, and track the Araketa back to its nest. Here I activate my Boost once again, and unleash a massively enhanced version of the Dual Blades signature Demon Flurry combo, landing dozens of hits in a matter of seconds, and ending with a massive pair of vertical slashes. It doesn’t take much more for the monster to fall.

The second, harder hunt on the docket is Teostra. This lion-headed Elder Dragon is a series staple, and has killed countless hunters, myself among them many times over the years. I switch to the Sword and Shield for this hunt, the extra protection will certainly be needed here, and bring along the Bow and Arrow as a secondary option, if fighting close the the fiery-based creature proves too dangerous.

This hunt takes us back to the Oilwell Basin. It doesn’t take any time to find the Teostra, this sort of beast doesn’t need to hide from anyone. Flames pour out of the side of the monster as I begin hacking away at him, using side steps and sliding slashes to try and stay away from his fangs and claws. I manage to mount him, and take him down to the ground with a mounted finisher. The sheer fury of relentless attacks l puts me on my heels, and his ability to set me on fire, or inflict blastblight, which will cause me to explode if I don’t clear the condition, has me juggling a lot more than just slashes and blocks. This is tough.

I activate my boost. My swordhand crackles with energy as I hold up my block and prepare a counterattack. I stave off two powerful swipes of Teostra’s tail and counter with an attack called a Spinning Reaper, a fast, backhand rotation with my blade for high damage. The Sword and Shield’s boost does a lot. Not only do I have new attacks, I also gain access to a ranged grapple move, similar to the Clutch Claw from Monster Hunter World: Iceborne. I also gain the ability to use items to coat my blade, allowing me to add new damage elements, or even a self-healing effect.

I knock Teostra down, activate my boost, and follow a three hit combo with a leap into the air, followed by a new version of the Falling Bash that sees me spiraling out of the air into the monster. Chaos of the fight aside, it’s easy to identify when your boost is ready, thanks to a distinctive locking-n-place sound effect, and boosted attacks are highlighted in a red font, with a boost icon next to the name of the move. But Teostra is relentless, and I lose too much potential offense to the time spent with my shield up. After 20 minutes, neither this monster nor I have fallen, but my time is up. Hunt failed.

The first taste of Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance already has me salivating. The new tricks, new (and returning) monsters, and brand new suite of boosts are going to significantly disrupt how I do my builds, and how I approach hunts. Just thinking about it now has my synapses firing, and there are still so many weapons who're boosted actions I have yet to try, and who knows what new armor set bonuses might be ahead of us. The endgame of Monster Hunter Wilds was too easy, but this might be what Monster Hunter sickos are looking for. We’ll know for sure when it launches sometimes in 2027.

articles.title: Yet Another Disney+ Price Hike Is Coming — and It's Reportedly Due This Week
articles.summary: Disney plans to raise the price of Disney+ this week, according to a new report.
articles.body:
Disney plans to raise the price of Disney+ this week, according to a new report.

Bloomberg said Disney+ without ads will go up by $2.50 — or 13% — to $21.49 per month. That’s closer to Netflix’s ad-free subscription, which costs $26.99 a month with 4K resolution and access on multiple devices.

According to the same report, Hulu without advertising is going up by the same amount. The ad-free subscription bundle including both Disney+ and Hulu increases by $2 to $21.99, or just 50 cents more than subscribing to each service individually.

Ranking the Star Wars Disney+ Live-Action TV Shows

The price rises are set to kick in today, Wednesday 23, for new subscribers, according to Bloomberg. Existing customers must pay the new prices from their next monthly bill. The ad-free Disney+ tier was just $10.99 a month just three years ago in 2023.

The news comes just days after Disney+ altered its user agreement for subscribers in Europe to clarify that ads will be allowed before and after playback on all subscription tiers . Subscribers in the U.S. have currently not received an updated agreement.

Disney+ has seen a number of price rises in recent years, most recently in October 2025. You can see the full line-up of content made available on the streaming service for September 2026 here .

articles.title: 72-Year-Old Pokémon Collector Arrested After Illegally Tracking Woman Who Restocked Local Stores
articles.summary: A 72-year-old Pokémon card collector has been arrested for illegally tracking a woman who restocked local stores.
articles.body:
A 72-year-old Pokémon card collector has been arrested for illegally tracking a woman who restocked local stores.

Cleveland resident Kent Kubasta has admitted following the woman's delivery route via an electronic tracker he had secretly placed on her vehicle, in order to see where new card boxes had been dropped off.

According to Fox8 , Kubasta entered a plea of no contest to the charge, and declined to comment further when approached by press for an explanation. It is assumed, however, that he was then planning to visit each store and buy up stock as soon as it was placed on sale.

POKÉMON COLLECTOR FOUND GUILTY FOR TRACKING A CARD VENDOR 🚨 A collector used a GPS tracker to follow a woman who stocked Pokémon cards, allowing him to track her route from store to store. Could’ve just turned notifications on 🤷‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/EpnYUPlg3a — Reselling News (@resellingnews) September 22, 2026

POKÉMON COLLECTOR FOUND GUILTY FOR TRACKING A CARD VENDOR 🚨 A collector used a GPS tracker to follow a woman who stocked Pokémon cards, allowing him to track her route from store to store. Could’ve just turned notifications on 🤷‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/EpnYUPlg3a

The tracker was discovered by the driver while dropping cards to a Walmart. A Spytech GPS, the device allowed someone — in this case Kubasta — to follow her movements in real-time via a linked smartphone app.

While word of when and where additional card stock will be available locally is of huge importance to fans struggling to get a hold of the in-demand cards, Kubasta's actions went beyond the usual sharing of intel via social media and online groups, or being tipped off by friendly store owners and delivery drivers. It was also just downright creepy.

Sentencing is yet to take place, but Kubasta could now face up to 180 days in jail and a $1,000 fine.

This month's release of the Pokémon trading card game's 30th Anniversary set has been marred by long lines , "ghost chairs" , in-person fights and now frustration from scalpers that rare cards are too easy to find . All of which is bad, except for that last one.

While the 30th Anniversary set has now launched, the next is not far behind. Earlier this week, IGN revealed three new card designs from the upcoming set Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution — Delta Reign set , a fresh batch of Mega Evolution-themed cards that is due out on November 6.

articles.title: Some Fans Seem to Think The Witcher 3 Remastered Looks Worse Than the Original in Official Comparison Clip
articles.summary: The Witcher 3 fans have reacted to an official comparison clip featuring a snippet of side-by-side gameplay from the original game and the upcoming remaster, with some saying the new version actually looks worse.
articles.body:
The Witcher 3 fans have reacted to an official comparison clip featuring a snippet of side-by-side gameplay from the original game and the upcoming remaster, with some saying the new version actually looks worse.

In the clip, you can see Geralt casting Igni on a group of drowners in the swamp, with a side-by-side comparison with the original game and the remaster. And while the new version of the game has much greater detail on Geralt's armor, along with much more defined water, the reflections seem to be divisive.

Choose your cast - wisely. #TheWitcher3Remastered pic.twitter.com/zcgLSvLvDi — The Witcher (@thewitcher) September 23, 2026

In the original game, you can see some of the fire reflected in the brackish water underneath the drowners, even if it results in an orange-ish blur. That'd be a pretty low bar to clear with the ray tracing on offer in the remaster, but the clip doesn't show any reflection of the fire at all. The fog is also much different in the remaster. In the original, there are defined clouds of fog floating just above the ground, where the remaster takes a more atmospheric approach to the fog in the distance.

A lot of the differences between the two sides of this clip comes down to the remaster using ray tracing, where the original didn't have it. Fans have had mixed reactions to this clip regardless. X / Twitter user LeafusMaximus said "despite literally adding RT to the game you managed to post a pic with worse water reflections, worse fog effects, worse armor textures in some cases (the glove he keeps back towards the camera for example), the new drowner just look wetter, the old ones actually look scaly/mucky." While desugar_64 simply asked: "Are you sure you didn't swap the footage around?"

Luckily, if you don't like the new visual representation, you should be able to roll back to an earlier version of the build as long as you're playing on PC. I'm not sure if that option will exist on consoles, but if you really don't want your current install of The Witcher 3 to get this change, you can turn off automatic updates. If you are planning on upgrading to the remaster though, you will be able to carry over your save data when the game comes out on September 29.

articles.title: Bethesda Boss Issues Memo to Staff After Xbox Moves Obsidian Into the Fallout Company
articles.summary: The boss of Bethesda has issued a memo to staff reassuring them that Obsidian Entertainment remains “distinct” despite being absorbed into the company as part of this week’s seismic Xbox studios reorganisation.
articles.body:
The boss of Bethesda has issued a memo to staff reassuring them that Obsidian Entertainment remains “distinct” despite being absorbed into the company as part of this week’s seismic Xbox studios reorganisation.

This week, Microsoft announced hundreds more layoffs as it gutted Halo Studios and handed the next mainline Halo game, Sea of Thieves developer Rare, and Age of Empires developer World's Edge to Activision . Meanwhile, Obsidian, the Microsoft-owned studio behind the likes of Grounded, The Outer Worlds, and Avowed, was made a part of Bethesda.

Obsidian, perhaps most famous for developing the much-loved Fallout: New Vegas, was confirmed to be working on a Fallout game in the wake of new Xbox boss Asha Sharma’s “reset” of Microsoft’s gaming business, which has seen nearly 2,000 staff cut in a bid for improved financial performance. More staff are set to lose their jobs over the course of the rest of the current financial year.

Bringing Obsidian into the Bethesda fold makes sense given it’s working on Fallout, but some had worried the move signalled an eventual relegation to Fallout support studio status. But in a memo to staff viewed by IGN, Bethesda boss Jill Braff insisted Obsidian would retain its leadership and identity, while confirming Bethesda Game Studios would “continue to lead the Fallout franchise.”

There is of course a huge amount going on at Bethesda right now, with The Elder Scrolls 6 the focus. Fallout 5 is in pre-production. BGS has also confirmed Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas remasters are in the works. No release windows are known for any of these games, nor Obsidian’s Fallout game.

Meanwhile, BGS has said Starfield "continues," although Bethesda stopped short of confirming a sequel is in the works.

The Xbox “reset” has left Xbox Game Studios a shadow of its former self, with a number of previously owned studios either independent, moved into Activision or Bethesda, or set for closure. Will Gears of War studio The Coalition, which suffered layoffs this week , Clockwork Revolution developer inXile, and Fable and Forza Horizon developer Playground eventually also end up at either Activision or Bethesda?

articles.body:
Years before he co-created 30 Days of Night, Steve Niles introduced the world to the hard-boiled paranormal detective known as Cal McDonald. Nearly 40 years later, Cal is making a big comeback, as Clover Press gears up to publish the new collection Cal McDonald: Plague of Evil and Other Stories.

With the Kickstarter campaign for Cal McDonald: Plague of Evil and Other Stories live now, IGN can exclusively debut a new preview of the book. Check out the slideshow gallery below for a look at the book's title story:

Cal McDonald: Plague of Evil and Other Stories Preview Gallery

Cal McDonald: Plague of Evil and Other Stories features ten new tales written by Niles, each accompanied by an illustration from a different comic book artist. The artists involved include Cat Staggs (John Carpenter’s Tales of Halloween Night), Liam Sharp (Star Henge), Scott Morse (Soulwind), Christopher Mitten (Hellboy and the BPRD), Gyula Nemeth (Criminal Macabre), Steven Russell Black (Magic The Gathering), Francesco Francavilla (The Black Beetle), Alison Sampson (Werewolf By Night), and Damien Worm (October Faction).

The book will be published through Clover Press' new creator-owned imprint, The Fourth Leaf. The company's press release teases, "In the tradition of Mickey Spillane and Raymond Chandler, Niles sends Cal and his undead sidekick on a strange journey through a Los Angeles populated by monsters, freaks, ghouls, and all kinds of new creatures hell-bent on causing chaos."

“It’s hard to believe but I’ve been writing Cal McDonald in one form or another for almost forty years now,” said Niles in a statement. “The last short story collection came out almost 20 years ago, so I am excited to have Plague of Evil coming out through Clover Press. Cal has always been my favorite character to write and it feels good to be back in the saddle again. I am especially thrilled with this volume because I have so many friends along for the ride; some of my favorite artists in the industry have added their talents. I hope readers enjoy this collection because I’m aching to do more.”
